extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians writing research papers (graduate students, postdocs, faculty); authors preparing LaTeX/arXiv submissions
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for producing clear, well-structured mathematical research papers (LaTeX/arXiv-centric), including framing, notation, references, figures, and post-publication steps. Targets clarity and readership rather than literary perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clear!
rubrics_metrics.description: This is the golden rule: clarity is absolutely paramount in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity is not just phrasing but a pervasive design goal that takes time and effort. The author emphasizes thinking about the reader, avoiding ambiguous notation, and investing effort to make the exposition unconfusing. Examples and consequences are provided (readers give up, lose citations, and your work can be ignored).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix notation inconsistencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve inconsistent uses of notation (e.g., the same symbol used as both variable and function) rather than relying on disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time (even 30 minutes) to rename symbols rather than writing section-specific disclaimers. Small notation confusions can lose readers; fixing them improves clarity and readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think of the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: Write with concrete reader types and reading behaviors in mind (grad students, postdocs, busy seniors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how different readers skim or read your paper; confusion early leads to abandonment. Clarity increases chance of adoption, citation, and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t rely on journals/copy editors for mathematical clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals and copy editors may catch linguistic issues but rarely resolve mathematical clarity problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most dissemination is via arXiv or personal web pages; authors should themselves ensure mathematical exposition is clear rather than hoping editors will fix it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignore style rules that harm clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: When standard grammar/style rules make math unclear, break them in favor of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try rewording first; if rules still impede clarity, override them (author gives amusing examples). The priority is reader comprehension over rigid adherence to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read existing guides and literature on mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Start by reading classical and modern guides (Halmos, Knuth, Krantz, Zinsser, etc.) before or alongside writing your paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different guides serve different needs: Zinsser for nonfiction craft, Halmos for math-specific brevity, Knuth for detailed mathematical writing, plus more recent online resources (Tao blog, others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt which guides you read to your background
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a native English speaker read Zinsser early; if not, start with Halmos and other short math-specific pieces and return to Zinsser later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advice is tailored: Zinsser is fundamental for natives; nonnative speakers may benefit from shorter math-focused guides first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clarity over perfect/old-fashioned style
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for clear and modern exposition rather than timeless perfection; modern readers have diverse skimming habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given rapid growth of literature and varied reader behaviors, favor a writing style that hooks and aids quick comprehension rather than stylistic perfection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure the paper as a Matryoshka doll
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide layers of information: a concise summary/abstract, a longer summary/introduction, and then full technical detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a super-brief summary, then expand; this helps readers with different depths of interest and matches common math-paper conventions (title, abstract, introduction, main part, final remarks, references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Title: concise, content-reflecting, tested
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a title that is neither too long nor too vague and that gives a first approximation to the paper's content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think long about titles, try versions on colleagues, use tricks like naming new objects for memorability, and choose phrasing that emphasizes what you want (e.g., 'All tennis balls are white' vs 'On white tennis balls'). Beware of naming credit issues and referees' reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: short MathSciNet-style summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a short, dry summary of key results (no personal commentary, no details), resembling a MathSciNet summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State main results and brief mention of others; avoid details and connections unless necessary. Rule of thumb: number of abstract lines ≈ 0.3–0.5 times the number of pages (e.g., 10-line abstract for 10 pages is excessive). Some journals advise no citations; but precision (e.g., citing your own work) can be acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents: omit for short papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include a table of contents unless the paper exceeds ~60 pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PDF readers provide navigation; a TOC is unnecessary for most papers and clutters short ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction: write the hardest section carefully and early
rubrics_metrics.description: The Introduction is the most-read section and should hook readers, set up the problem, and state main results early (ideally a theorem on page 1–2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a senior coauthor or colleague comment; draft the Introduction first and rewrite after completing the paper; include essential technical definitions only if few; use easily stated corollaries as advertisements; avoid long technicalities and relegate details to the body or Final Remarks; end the Introduction with an outline of the paper's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a Foreword for long introductions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Introduction becomes long (>~3–4 pages), include a Foreword subsection to give a nontechnical overview and big-picture motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreword can include literary/philosophical motivation and may be quoted elsewhere; keep it under a page if possible. Even short papers can benefit from an opening paragraph in this style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Remarks: use as expanded endnotes ordered by importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat Final Remarks as endnotes/expanded footnotes divided into short untitled subsections ordered by importance (history, applications, conjectures, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Final Remarks to host material referenced from the main text (placeholders in earlier sections linking to Final Remarks), allow updates on arXiv, and organize content so interested readers can click to details without cluttering the main exposition. Options to manage length: create new sections (Open problems, Historical overview), keep full version on arXiv/website, or typeset Final Remarks in smaller font.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements: order and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a short unnumbered Acknowledgements section before References; proceed in order of increasing importance and list conversational contributors alphabetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name people (nicknames acceptable) alphabetically, single out those who gave major help with brief explanations, include institutions and grant support, and ask permission before including private information.

rubrics_metrics.name: References matter greatly
rubrics_metrics.description: References are critical to the scholarly ecosystem and citations; they deserve careful, fair treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations cost the author little but affect others' careers; sloppy or unfair referencing can have negative consequences. The author provides a passionate rationale for careful referencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to cite a single paper: phrasing conveys reliability/meaning (list of forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different phrasings of a citation carry distinct connotations about priority, reliability, and the nature of the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The note lists many formulations and their implied meanings (examples 1–12), from 'Roth proved X in [Roth].' (clear definitive claim) to 'Roth claims to have proved X in [Roth].' (possible gap or dubious). Choose phrasing to reflect what you actually know about the cited work (definitive proof, survey, partial result, personal communication, claim only, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to cite multiple papers: describe contributions individually
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lumping references as 'See [2–19]' — instead summarize each important work's contribution in order of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide brief descriptions of what each cited paper contributes, and place such detailed history in Final Remarks while keeping the Introduction focused on the most relevant references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to place citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite the most relevant papers in the Introduction; place the rest in Final Remarks; cite in the main body only when using a result as a lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid breaking flow by excessive mid-proof citations. For narrative commentary or credit, use Remarks or Final Remarks. This also makes updating references on the arXiv easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form references to stable locations (use arXiv section numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting specific results from long documents, reference stable locations like section/subsection numbers in arXiv versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: arXiv numbering tends to be stable compared to preliminary electronic versions; cite e.g. '[A, §3.1]'. This may contradict some publisher guidelines but is practical for locating statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style of references: concise, consistent, and practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a consistent, concise reference style; avoid BibTeX unless you know how to manage it; use alphanumeric labels for long papers; include arXiv numbers and short URLs for unpublished work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bloated MathSciNet styles and inconsistent author name formats. For many authors use [A+13]; differentiate same-author-year with letters [Tra15a], [Tra15b]. Use https links and URL-shorteners to make links tidy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow basic grammar but avoid pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhere to standard grammar guides but avoid over-explaining trivial or standard mathematical notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult recommended grammar/style references for rules, but do not be pedantic to the point of harming clarity or slowing exposition (e.g., avoid overexplaining standard terms; a picture may suffice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Downshift your style for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer clear, simple vocabulary and repetitive reminders over varied high-style prose; use short sentences and present tense primarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be repetitive if it aids reader comprehension, use present indefinite tense, keep sentences short, employ commas to show structure, avoid semicolons and overcomplicated words, and favor Standard American English spelling for broad accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX: create and reuse macros; keep notation consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Define many macros for symbols and notation, reuse them across papers, and use placeholders while drafting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macros speed typing and allow global notation changes. Create mnemonics for macros, standardize which letters denote functions/constants/integers, avoid visually confusing glyphs, and experiment with fonts at the end to avoid clashes. Use caution with exotic alphabets and gothic fonts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do NOT trust LaTeX's default output blindly
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspect compiled output for spacing/formatting ambiguities; adjust manually where LaTeX layout creates confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert manual spacing (e.g., '\,') to avoid ambiguous runs of symbols; ensure formulas and compact numeric sequences are readable (e.g., separate partition parts with spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures: many but small; avoid oversized detailed figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use many small figures (3–5 cm) rather than few huge, overly detailed figures that break flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If details are necessary, create multiple aligned copies with progressively more detail, or move large figures to appendix/website and link to them. Readers can zoom if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the paper stew and solicit feedback before wide release
rubrics_metrics.description: After finishing, wait (a week), solicit colleagues' feedback, fix typos and substantive issues, then put on arXiv; continue updating as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rush to arXiv immediately; collect comments from trusted colleagues and correct issues. For serious published mistakes (wrong proof, missing attribution) issue an Erratum or Acknowledgement of attribution as a separate file.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertise and popularize the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase accessibility by linking recorded talks/slides and writing blog posts or expository pieces; extract simple special cases for competitions or student-oriented journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Link talks next to the paper, write short blog summaries, prepare olympiad-style problems or accessible notes for undergraduate venues (Amer. Math. Monthly, Math. Intelligencer) to broaden reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite and republish when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper is being ignored due to unclear exposition, rewrite and publish an improved, possibly more specialized or pedagogical version (including on arXiv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may present a clear proof of a known simpler case followed by generalization to get both clarity and novelty; republishing improved exposition is acceptable to increase impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Final Remarks / arXiv for dynamic updates and staking claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep Final Remarks expandable on arXiv and your website to add new material, conjectures, or outlines of solutions without changing the main paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can serve as a dynamic semi-survey or place to announce ideas to deter competition; keep theorems/proofs intact in published versions and use Erratum for substantive corrections.
